interactive.title: The drop inside the windings
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Fourteen small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and nine ask you to try it.

The picture. Last lesson's 10 kVA, 440 V to 115 V transformer, single-phase, seen from its 115 V side: windings' resistance 4%, leakage reactance 3%, impedance 5%. On the left, a phasor diagram zoomed in on the tip of the output arrow, true to scale, its axis from 102 V to 117 V. The Output arrow lies along the axis. From its tip, the I × R arrow points along the current, then the I × X arrow a quarter-turn ahead of it. The last tip sits on an arc of the fixed 115 V circle, labelled Supply. A tick marks 115 V on the axis, the no-load tip. A short Current arrow shows the current's direction. On the right, from the impedance screen on, a fault-current bar, 0 to 5000 A.

The controls, each shown only where a screen uses it. A load slider, 0 to 125% in steps of 5, opening at 100. A power factor stepper with seven settings, in this order: 0.5 lag, 0.6 lag, 0.8 lag, 1.0, 0.8 lead, 0.6 lead, 0.5 lead. It opens at 1.0, and its buttons wrap onto two rows on a phone. An impedance slider, 2 to 10% in steps of 0.5, opening at 5.

The rules. Rated current = 10,000 ÷ 115 = 86.96 A. Load fraction x = slider ÷ 100. The impedance slider sets Z%, and R% = 0.8 × Z% and X% = 0.6 × Z%, so the 4 to 3 ratio holds. The drop's size d = Z% ÷ 100 × 115 × x, in V: 5.75 V at full load and 5%. Its two parts are R% ÷ 100 × 115 × x along the current, 4.6 V at full load, and X% ÷ 100 × 115 × x a quarter-turn ahead, 3.45 V. The load angle φ = arccos(power factor), positive lagging, negative leading: 36.9° at 0.8. The windings' own angle is 36.9° too, as 3.45 ÷ 4.6 = 0.75. The drop points at the windings' angle minus φ, called α, from the output. The tip must land on the 115 V circle, so Output = √(115² − (d sin α)²) − d cos α, in V. Regulation = (115 − Output) ÷ 115 × 100, in %. Rule = x × (R% cos φ + X% sin φ), in %, with sin φ negative when leading. Fault current = 86.96 × 100 ÷ Z%, in A.

The readouts, wrapping onto two rows on a phone, each shown only from the screen that brings it in: Output, V, two decimal places; Regulation, %, one decimal place; Rule, %, one decimal place; Fault current, A, whole amps. At full load and 5%: 110.35 V and 4.0% at 1.0; 109.25 V and 5.0% at 0.8 lag; 113.26 V and 1.5% at 0.8 lead; 115.55 V and −0.5% at 0.5 lead. The rule gives 4.0, 5.0, 1.4 and −0.6%. The fault current is 1739 A at 5%, 3478 A at 2.5% and 870 A at 10%.

Screen 1, try it, a recall, typed. "Two voltages in series: 6 V at 0° and 8 V at 90°. What is their total size?" Typed, in V, whole numbers: answer 10, want "10 V". Slips: 14, "That adds them straight. At right angles they add like a triangle's sides."; 2, "That takes one from the other. They are at right angles, not opposed." Hint otherwise: "Square each, add, then take the root." Why: "√(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 V. The drops inside a transformer add the same way." A right Check says "Still there." and carries on. Read: "Two voltages in series are 6 V at 0° and 8 V at 90°. What is their total size?"

Screen 2, show. The load slider to drag, and no readouts yet. The words: "Loading shortens the output. Off load there is no load current, so the windings drop almost nothing. The output reaches the 115 V circle. Drag the load up. The current drops a voltage across the windings' resistance, in line with the current. It drops another across their reactance, a quarter-turn ahead of it. Both sit tip to tail on the output arrow. The supply fixes the circle. So the output must shorten to keep the last tip on it." Read: "Off load the output reaches the 115 V circle. On load, two drops sit tip to tail on the output arrow. One is across the windings' resistance, the other across their reactance. The last tip stays on the circle, so the output shortens." Still: load 100%, power factor 1.0.

Screen 3, try it, typed. "At full load and unity power factor, the drop has two parts. It is 4.6 V in line with the output and 3.45 V at right angles to it. The supply's circle is 115 V. What is the output, to two decimal places?" Typed, in V, two decimal places: answer 110.35, want "110.35 V". Only the output readout shows, and it shows ? until Check. Slips: 106.95, "That takes both drops straight off. The 3.45 V is at right angles, so it costs little."; 109.25, "That takes the whole 5.75 V straight off. At unity the drop is not in line with the output."; 110.4, "That is close. Work the triangle to two decimal places." Hint otherwise: "Make a right-angled triangle with 115 V as its long side. Its short sides are the output plus 4.6 V, and the 3.45 V across." Why: "√(115² − 3.45²) = 114.95 V along the axis. The 3.45 V across costs only 0.05 V. Take off the 4.6 V: 110.35 V." Read: "At full load and unity power factor, the drop is 4.6 V in line with the output and 3.45 V across it. The arrows close on 115 V. What is the output, to two decimal places?"

Screen 4, show. The power factor stepper, with the output and regulation readouts. The regulation readout shows ? at 1.0 and at 0.5 lead, as later puzzles ask for those. The words: "For this transformer, 0.8 lagging gives the deepest sag. The whole drop points 36.9° ahead of the current. That is the windings' own angle, set by 3.45 against 4.6. Step the power factor to 0.8 lagging. The current swings back 36.9°, so the drop lines up with the output. The whole 5.75 V comes straight off, leaving 109.25 V. [[Voltage regulation]] is the sag as a share of the no-load voltage. Here it is 5.75 ÷ 115 = 5.0%." Read: "At 0.8 lagging the drop lines up with the output. The whole 5.75 V comes off, leaving 109.25 V. Regulation is the sag as a share of the no-load voltage: 5.0%." Still: load 100%, power factor 0.8 lag.

Screen 5, try it, typed. The picture: load 100%, power factor 1.0. "At unity power factor the output is 110.35 V. At no load it is 115 V. What is the regulation?" Typed, in %, one decimal place: answer 4.0, want "4.0%". The regulation readout shows ? until Check. Slips: 4.2, "That divides by the on-load 110.35 V. Regulation divides by the no-load 115 V."; 5.0, "That is the figure at 0.8 lagging. At unity the reactance drop points straight across, so it costs almost nothing." Hint otherwise: "(115 − 110.35) ÷ 115 × 100." Why: "4.65 ÷ 115 = 0.040, so 4.0%. It is less than at 0.8 lagging. Here the 3.45 V points across the output." Read: "At unity power factor the output is 110.35 V against 115 V at no load. What is the regulation?"

Screen 6, try it, a prediction. The picture: load 100%, power factor 1.0, the output readout only. "Before you see it, predict. At full load, will 0.8 leading sag more or less than unity?" Three choices, in this order: "More than at unity"; "Less than at unity"; "The same as at unity". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "Leading swings the current forward, not back. The drop swings forward with it, away from the output." Hint for the third: "The drop swings with the current. So its part along the output changes too." Why: "A leading current swings the drop forward, away from the output. Less of the drop then lies along the output. So the output sags less than at unity." Read: "Before you see it, predict. At full load, will 0.8 leading sag more or less than unity?"

Screen 7, show. The power factor stepper and the output readout only. The words: "A leading load raises the output.[^1] Step on to leading. The drop swings forward, so less of it lies along the output. At 0.8 leading the output is 113.26 V. That is a regulation of 1.5%. At 0.6 leading the drop points straight across. Past that it points back against the output. Soon the output passes 115 V to reach the circle. At 0.5 leading it is 115.55 V." Read: "With a leading load, less of the drop lies along the output, so the output rises. It is 113.26 V at 0.8 leading. Past 0.6 leading the drop points back. At 0.5 leading the output is 115.55 V, above no load." Still: load 100%, power factor 0.5 lead.

Screen 8, try it, typed. The picture: load 100%, power factor 0.5 lead. "At 0.5 leading the output reads 115.55 V. At no load it is 115 V. What is the regulation?" Typed, in %, one decimal place: answer −0.5, want "−0.5%". The regulation readout shows ? until Check. Slips: 0.5, "The output rose above no load. So no-load minus on-load is negative." Hint otherwise: "(115 − 115.55) ÷ 115 × 100." Why: "−0.55 ÷ 115 = −0.0048, so −0.5%. Negative regulation means the output rose on load." Read: "At 0.5 leading the output is 115.55 V against 115 V at no load. What is the regulation?"

Screen 9, show. The power factor stepper, with the output, regulation and Rule readouts. The words: "A quick rule counts only the parts of the drops along the output. I × R sits at φ to it, giving IR cos φ. I × X is a quarter-turn further on, giving IX sin φ. As shares, regulation ≈ R% cos φ + X% sin φ. Take sin φ as negative when leading. R% is also the full-load copper loss over the rating, since I²R ÷ VI = IR ÷ V. With R% at 4 and X% at 3, 0.8 leading gives 3.2 − 1.8 = 1.4%." Read: "Regulation ≈ R% cos φ + X% sin φ, the parts of the two drops along the output. Take sin φ as negative when leading. R% is the full-load copper loss as a share of the rating. With R% at 4 and X% at 3, that gives 5.0% at 0.8 lagging and 1.4% at 0.8 leading." Still: load 100%, power factor 0.8 lead.

Screen 10, try it, typed. "Another transformer has an R% of 1.5 and an X% of 3. What is its regulation at full load, 0.8 lagging?" Typed, in %, one decimal place: answer 3.0, want "3.0%". Slips: 4.5, "That adds them straight. Weight R% by cos φ and X% by sin φ."; 3.3, "That swaps them. R% goes with cos φ, which is 0.8."; −0.6, "That is the leading figure. Lagging, X% sin φ adds." Hint otherwise: "R% × 0.8 + X% × 0.6." Why: "1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2 and 3 × 0.6 = 1.8. Together that is 3.0%." Read: "A transformer has an R% of 1.5 and an X% of 3. What is its regulation at full load, 0.8 lagging?"

Screen 11, show. The impedance slider to drag. The fault-current bar and readout appear here. The words: "One impedance sets both the sag and the fault current. [[Percentage impedance]] is the share of rated voltage that drives rated current through a shorted secondary. Last lesson's short-circuit test measured it: 22.0 V of 440 V, so 5%. Full voltage on that short drives 100 ÷ 5 = 20 times rated current.[^2] Rated current is 86.96 A. With a stiff supply, a short at the terminals draws 1739 A. Drag the impedance down. The drops shrink and the output holds up, but the fault bar grows.[^3]" Read: "Percentage impedance is the share of rated voltage that drives rated current through a short. Here it is 5%. So with a stiff supply, full voltage drives 20 times rated current, 1739 A. A lower impedance gives less drop and more fault current." Still: load 100%, power factor 0.8 lag, impedance 5%.

Screen 12, try it, typed. No picture. "A 20 kVA, 115 V transformer has 4% impedance. What current flows into a dead short at its terminals?" Typed, in A, whole numbers: answer 4348, accepting 4350, want "4348 A". Slips: 696, "That multiplies by 4. Divide 100 by the impedance first."; 2174, "That is the figure for 10 kVA. Find this unit's own rated current first." Hint otherwise: "Rated current = 20,000 ÷ 115. Then multiply by 100 ÷ Z%." Why: "20,000 ÷ 115 = 173.91 A rated. 100 ÷ 4 = 25, and 173.91 × 25 = 4348 A. Twice the rating at the same impedance gives twice the fault current." Read: "A 20 kVA, 115 V transformer has 4% impedance. What current flows into a dead short at its terminals?"

Screen 13, try it, the first of two mixed puzzles, typed. "A transformer has an R% of 2 and an X% of 4. What is its regulation at full load, 0.8 leading?" Typed, in %, one decimal place: answer −0.8, want "−0.8%". Slips: 0.8, "When leading, sin φ counts as negative. So X% sin φ comes off."; 4.0, "That is the lagging figure. Leading, X% sin φ comes off."; −2.0, "That swaps them. R% goes with cos φ, which is 0.8." Hint otherwise: "2 × 0.8 − 4 × 0.6." Why: "1.6 − 2.4 = −0.8%. The output rises a little above no load." Read: "A transformer has an R% of 2 and an X% of 4. What is its regulation at full load, 0.8 leading?"

Screen 14, try it, the second mixed puzzle. "A board needs a small volt drop and a low fault current. You can fit a 4% or an 8% transformer of the same rating. Which is true of the two?" Four choices, in this order: "8% gives less drop and less fault current"; "4% gives less drop and less fault current"; "4% gives less drop, 8% less fault current"; "8% gives less drop, 4% less fault current". Right, the third. Hint for the first: "More impedance drops more volts, so the 8% unit sags more." Hint for the second: "Halving the impedance doubles the fault current." Hint for the fourth: "That is the wrong way round. Less impedance, less drop." Why: "The 8% unit's drop is about twice the 4% unit's. Its fault current is about half. One impedance cannot make both small. So you choose by which limit is tighter." Read: "A board needs a small volt drop and a low fault current. You can fit a 4% or an 8% transformer of the same rating. Which is true of the two?"

The finish. The words: "Current through the windings drops a voltage that sits tip to tail on the output. The sag is deepest when the load lags at the windings' own angle. A leading load can lift the output above no load. Percentage impedance sets both the sag and the fault current. Less of one means more of the other. Next: three-phase transformers and their clock."
interactive.ignores: The supply is taken as stiff. Its own impedance is left out, so the 115 V circle never moves. A real supply and the cables after the transformer add impedance. So a real fault usually draws less than the figure shown. The core's small magnetising current is left out, as in last lesson's approximate circuit. The windings' resistance is held fixed. Real copper's resistance rises as it warms. The impedance slider keeps resistance and reactance in the same 4 to 3 ratio. A real design of another impedance would have its own ratio. The fault current is the steady rms current. In the first cycle of a real fault the current can peak higher. The load is single-phase. Every voltage and current is rms.

explain.text:
A transformer's output sags as you load it. The load current flows through the windings' resistance and leakage reactance. Each one drops a voltage. The power factor decides how far the output sags. A lagging load sags it most. A leading load can even lift it. The same impedance limits the current a short at the terminals can draw. So less sag comes with more fault current.

Take last lesson's 10 kVA, 440 V to 115 V transformer, seen from its 115 V side. Off load there is no load current, so the windings drop almost nothing. The output is the full 115 V that the supply fixes. Full load is 86.96 A. That current drops 4.6 V across the windings' resistance, in line with the current. It drops 3.45 V across their reactance. That drop sits a quarter-turn ahead of the current, as in any inductor. The drops add tip to tail onto the output. The total must still be 115 V. At unity power factor the 3.45 V points across the output. Pointing across, it only tilts the output and costs just 0.05 V. So the output is √(115² − 3.45²) − 4.6 = 110.35 V. The whole drop points 36.9° ahead of the current. That is the windings' own angle, set by 3.45 against 4.6. At 0.8 lagging the current swings back 36.9°. Now the drop lines up with the output and comes straight off: 115 − 5.75 = 109.25 V. Lead the current and the drop swings the other way. Less of it then lies along the output. Past 0.6 leading it points back against the output. Soon the output passes 115 V to keep the total the same. At 0.5 leading it is 115.55 V. So a leading load raises the output, and a lagging one lowers it.[^1]

[[Voltage regulation]] is the sag as a share of the no-load voltage: (no-load − on-load) ÷ no-load × 100. Here it is 4.0% at unity, 5.0% at 0.8 lagging and −0.5% at 0.5 leading. A smaller figure means a steadier voltage. A quick rule gives it without the drawing: R% cos φ + X% sin φ. Take sin φ as negative when leading. R% is the full-load copper loss as a share of the rating. Here that is 400 W of 10 kVA, so 4%. With X% at 3%, the rule gives 5.0% at 0.8 lagging.

[[Percentage impedance]] is the share of rated voltage that drives rated current through a shorted secondary. Last lesson's short-circuit test measured it: 22.0 V of 440 V, so 5%. Full voltage on that short drives 100 ÷ 5 = 20 times rated current.[^2] Here that is 86.96 × 20 = 1739 A at the 115 V terminals. Build the same transformer with 2.5% and its sag halves. But its fault current doubles to 3478 A. This picture is simplified. It takes the supply as stiff and leaves out the core's small current. **A lower impedance can give better regulation, but it also lets more current into a downstream fault.[^3]**

analogy.text: Think of the volt-drop sum for a large cable at a power factor. You take the resistive part times cos φ and the reactive part times sin φ, then add. Regulation's quick rule is the same sum. The windings simply take the cable's place. And as with a cable, the one that drops the fewest volts lets the most fault current through.
analogy.breaks: A cable's impedance changes with its length and size. You can change it by changing the run. A transformer's impedance is fixed when it is built. You read it off its plate. Its R and X come from its own tests, not from a cable table. R comes from the copper loss, and Z from the short-circuit test.

practice.text:
**Safe way first:** Work out the fault current at the terminals before you choose the protective devices. Each device's breaking capacity must be at least the prospective fault current where it is fitted. A lower-impedance transformer raises that figure.

**Steps:**
- Read the rating, the secondary voltage and the impedance, Z%, from the plate. The plate may call Z% the impedance voltage.[^4]
- Get R% from the copper loss: full-load copper loss ÷ rating × 100. Then X% = √(Z%² − R%²).
- Rated current = rating ÷ secondary voltage.
- Regulation at full load ≈ R% cos φ + X% sin φ. Take sin φ as negative when leading. At part load, multiply by the load fraction.
- On-load voltage ≈ no-load voltage × (1 − regulation ÷ 100).
- With a stiff supply, fault current at the terminals = rated current × 100 ÷ Z%.

**Rules of thumb:** The sag is deepest when the load's angle matches the windings' own. Then the regulation is the whole Z% at full load. A leading load can lift the output above no load. Halve the impedance and the fault current at the terminals about doubles.

**Worked example:** A 10 kVA, 115 V transformer has 5% impedance. That is 4% resistance and 3% reactance. Rated current is 10,000 ÷ 115 = 86.96 A. At 0.8 lagging the regulation is 4 × 0.8 + 3 × 0.6 = 5.0%. So the output is about 115 × 0.95 = 109.25 V. At unity the regulation is 4.0%, giving about 110.4 V. A short at its terminals draws about 86.96 × 20 = 1739 A. A 2.5% unit of the same size, with the same 4 to 3 split of R and X, sags only 2.5% at 0.8 lagging. But it lets 3478 A into the same short.

**Common mistakes**
- Dividing by the on-load voltage. Regulation is a share of the no-load voltage.
- Forgetting the sign of sin φ for a leading load. Regulation can be negative.
- Adding R% and X% straight. They are at right angles, so Z% = √(R%² + X%²).
- Taking a higher impedance as better all round. It lowers the fault current. But it deepens the sag.
- Using the terminal figure far downstream. The cables' impedance lowers the fault current further along.

applied.problem: "Past 0.6 leading ... the output must pass 115 V" is not literally true: with the drop pointing just behind square the output is still a hair under 115 V; at full load it crosses 115 V only near 0.58 leading (cos α = −d/230), so it passes 115 V a little further on.

Screen 6 repeats the claim that once the drop points back the output must pass 115 V (it crosses only near 0.58 leading at full load); screen 13's why says the 8% drop is exactly twice and the fault current exactly half, true only for the same resistance-to-reactance mix and a stiff supply.

Read alone, "draws up to 1739 A" and "halve the impedance and the fault current doubles" overstate: a plate impedance carries a tolerance and a supply can run above nominal, while a real supply's impedance makes halving Z% less than double the current; both are stiff-supply terminal figures.

"Which is the most a short at the terminals can draw" is too absolute for the real world: a plate impedance has a manufacturing tolerance and the supply can sit above nominal, so a real terminal fault can exceed the stiff-supply figure; the cables-and-supply point only makes a real fault usually sm…
